strengths: The paper targets a relevant and underexplored threat model: a non-invasive, 3D-consistent adversarial object that attacks BEV-based multi-camera 3D detectors without modifying the target vehicle, which is a meaningful extension over invasive camouflage methods and 2D patch attacks.

The technical pipeline is sensible and well-motivated: differentiable mesh rendering (PyTorch3D) for multi-view consistency, an occlusion-aware compositing module using SAM2 to model realistic partial visibility, and a BEV feature-guided loss (target suppression + localization disruption + scene confusion) for cross-view/cross-frame attack effectiveness.

The experimental coverage is comparatively thorough: three victim models (BEVDet, BEVDet4D, BEVFormer), multiple IoU thresholds for ASR, ablations over mesh shape, attack distance, random placement, realistic occlusion, plus appendix studies on transferability across models and distance robustness.

The 'Real Occ' ablation and the Init-vs-Adv comparison help disentangle attack effectiveness from the trivial effect of merely inserting an object, and the limitation section honestly reports failure cases (e.g., weak performance on BEVDet4D and under random placement).
weaknesses: Evaluation is entirely in simulation (nuScenes with rendered meshes); despite claims of 'real-world attack scenarios' and 'deployable setup', no physical-world or even photorealistic rendering validation is provided, leaving the practical realism of the threat model unverified.

A potential confound remains insufficiently addressed: inserting a large object near a vehicle in multi-view images could suppress detection through apparent occlusion or out-of-distribution appearance regardless of adversarial optimization. The Init vs. Adv gap supports the attack, but there is no control experiment with a non-optimized random-texture object of the same geometry, so the attribution of success to learned adversarial textures is not fully established.

The comparison with Adv3d in Table 2 is not apples-to-apples: the baseline's initial NDS/mAP (0.2820/0.1727) differs substantially from the authors' setup (0.3579/0.2625), suggesting different evaluation configurations, and the two methods have different objectives (whole-scene degradation vs. targeted suppression), making the 'superior adversarial strength' claim hard to assess.

Multiple technical inconsistencies undermine clarity and confidence: Eq. 1 is called an attack loss to be minimized while the text says to maximize prediction error, with unclear sign conventions (also in Eq. 5); the occlusion depth condition 'If dk < bmesh' should presumably be d_mesh (a variable named 'bmesh' is undefined); and the broken LaTeX macro 'i.elet@tokeneonedot' appears repeatedly throughout the paper, along with unfinished-looking red text in Sec. 4.3.

The claim of 'universal adversarial objects' is overstated: objects are optimized in a white-box manner against each victim model and their effectiveness drops sharply under random placement (ASR 0.13–0.13 with a single randomly placed mesh) and against BEVDet4D, as the authors themselves acknowledge in the limitations.

No code or reproducibility statement is provided; given the pipeline's many components (placement heuristics, SAM2 prompting, rendering details, loss weighting), reproducing the results without a release would be difficult.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a camera-ready submission: figures and tables are dense and occasionally hard to parse (e.g., Tables 4/5 formatting, Table 8 column alignment), and the method section's notation drifts (p_m, d, n-hat conventions) in ways that require careful reverse-engineering by the reader.

strengths: The problem is safety-relevant and well-motivated: probing the robustness of BEV-based 3D detectors to non-invasive, spatially consistent adversarial objects is a legitimate and under-explored threat model compared to invasive camouflage attacks.

The evaluation effort is reasonably broad for an attack paper: three victim detectors (BEVDet, BEVDet4D, BEVFormer), ablations over mesh shape and occlusion handling, transfer attacks across models (Appendix B), and distance/placement robustness studies (Tab. 4, 5, 9).

The paper is candid in several places, e.g., acknowledging that BEVDet4D resists the attack, that random single-mesh placement largely fails (Tab. 5, ASR 0.13), and that the initialized object itself shifts predictions (Sec. 4.5).

The occlusion-aware rendering module (SAM2-based masking with depth-based ordering) is a practical engineering addition over Adv3D's crude pasting and helps the attack better approximate realistic multi-view occlusion.
weaknesses: Limited novelty over the closest baseline Adv3D [17]: the core recipe (differentiably rendered 3D content optimized against a BEV detector) is shared; the delta is a mesh representation instead of NeRF plus an occlusion module. Given the long lineage of adversarial meshes (Athalye et al. [31], MeshAdv [29]), the conceptual contribution is incremental.

The evaluation contains a serious confound that undermines the central claim. The 'Init' condition already degrades clean performance substantially (e.g., BEVDet: clean NDS 0.3942 vs. Init 0.3579; Table 3 shows even larger gaps for cube/sphere), meaning a large fraction of the reported 'attack' effect may simply come from inserting any object near the target rather than from adversarial optimization. The paper acknowledges this in Sec. 4.5 but never quantifies how much of the drop is attributable to the adversarial objective itself.

The occlusion ablation weakens the realism claim: when the 'Realistic Occlusion' module is enabled, ASR drops sharply (e.g., BEVDet 0.613 → 0.447; cylinder in Tab. 3), suggesting the attack relies significantly on unrealistic, occlusion-free renderings. The headline numbers are largely from the unrealistic setting.

No physical or real-world experiments. Despite claims of 'real-world attack scenarios' and 'deployable setup', everything is digital insertion into nuScenes images; lighting, printer/material effects, and viewpoint jitter—critical for physical adversarial objects—are untested.

The 'universal' generalization claim is only weakly supported: with one randomly placed mesh the ASR is 0.175/0.130 (Tab. 5), and Appendix C shows the attack degrades monotonically as placement moves from the training location. The attack is highly placement-dependent, which contradicts the abstract's framing.

Metric and comparison concerns: (a) ASR increases with stricter IoU thresholds (0.594 at 0.2 up to 0.715 at 0.7 in Tab. 1), which is counterintuitive and never explained, suggesting an artifact of the ASR definition; (b) in Tab. 2, 'Ours' and Adv3d start from very different Init NDS (0.3579 vs. 0.2820), so the direct comparison of Adv numbers is not controlled; (c) no comparison to other patch-based baselines such as [15, 16].

Technical sloppiness that should not appear at this venue: the broken LaTeX macro 'i.elet@tokeneonedot' appears repeatedly in the abstract, introduction, and Eq. 1 discussion; a typo 'dk < bmesh' in the depth-occlusion condition; Eq. 5's L_loc uses the model's predicted box in an underspecified way (the prediction during optimization is not defined); the L_sim term (Eq. 6) is labeled 'minimizing cosine similarity' to 'encourage false positives' without any analysis connecting global BEV feature divergence to false positives.

The occlusion module itself is heuristic: it compares only mesh-vertex depth against the minimum 3D box-corner depth per object, then masks with SAM2 prompted by projected 2D boxes. This will fail for partially occluding thin objects or non-annotated clutter, yet no failure analysis is provided.

Writing quality is below CVPR bar in places: inconsistent terminology ('micro-renderable setup'), missing article usage, tables with cramped notation (Tab. 6-8 headers), and figure/section references that assume content not clearly presented (e.g., Fig. 3 discussion relies on a 'first row' that is hard to parse).

strengths: The paper targets a relevant and under-explored threat model: a non-invasive, spatially consistent 3D adversarial object that attacks BEV-based multi-view 3D detectors without modifying the target vehicle. This is a meaningful distinction from prior camouflage-style attacks (Fig. 1) and from Adv3d's NeRF-based object insertion.

The technical pipeline is sensible and mostly well-motivated: differentiable mesh rendering (PyTorch3D) for cross-view consistency, a SAM2-based occlusion handling module to keep rendered perturbations realistic under partial visibility, and a BEV feature-guided loss (Eq. 7) that combines target suppression, localization disruption, and scene confusion.

The evaluation is comparatively broad for an attack paper: three victim detectors (BEVDet, BEVDet4D, BEVFormer-small), ASR at multiple IoU thresholds plus NDS/mAP, a direct comparison to Adv3d, ablations over mesh shape, attack distance, number of randomly placed meshes, plus transfer attack experiments and per-range AP analysis in the appendix.

The paper is honest about limitations: weak performance on BEVDet4D and under random single-mesh placement are explicitly discussed, and the sensitivity of results to the occlusion module is exposed in the ablations (Tab. 3).
weaknesses: The formulation has material inconsistencies that make the method hard to verify. Eq. 1 introduces an Lp-bounded perturbation delta on images, but the method actually optimizes mesh vertices V and textures T; the constraint is never used. Eq. 5 is described as maximizing localization discrepancy, yet the overall objective (Eq. 7) is a minimization, and the sign of Lloc makes the intended direction ambiguous. Notation errors (e.g., 'd_k < b_mesh' on page 5, which should be d_mesh) further undermine confidence.

The ASR metric (ASR = 1 - Nadv/Ninit) is problematic. Inserting a non-adversarial mesh ('Init') already causes substantial degradation relative to clean performance (clean NDS 0.3942 vs. Init NDS 0.3579 on BEVDet, Tab. 3), so a large fraction of the reported ASR may reflect generic occlusion/insertion artifacts rather than adversarial effectiveness. The Real Occ ablation (ASR drops from ~0.61 to ~0.45) confirms the attack relies partly on unrealistic occlusion handling. A clean baseline without any object, and an analysis of ASR attributable purely to the adversarial texture, is needed.

The comparison with Adv3d (Tab. 2) is confounded: Adv3d achieves a lower Adv mAP (0.0967 vs. 0.1298) and lower Adv NDS (0.2277 vs. 0.2097), i.e., a stronger overall attack, while the paper claims superiority based on targeted AP_car. The different Init baselines (0.3579 vs. 0.2820) suggest different experimental setups, making the comparison hard to interpret.

Generality of the threat is limited: the attack fails badly with a single randomly placed mesh (ASR0.3 = 0.175, Tab. 5), is weak against the temporally consistent BEVDet4D (ASR0.2 = 0.29), and is entirely simulation-based with no physical-world or even rendering-pipeline validation (lighting/material consistency is acknowledged as a problem). The claim of a 'universal' object overstated given these results.

Presentation quality is below CVPR standards: the broken macro 'i.elet@tokeneonedot' appears throughout, unresolved red text is visible in figure captions and body text (e.g., 'Fig. 3', 'Placeability' style edits on pages 4, 6, 8, 9), and the title/name ('Meeseeks Mesh') plus jargon like 'micro-renderable setup' are used without definition. No code release is mentioned, which hurts reproducibility for an attack/robustness-evaluation paper.

Novelty relative to Adv3d is incremental: the core idea (insert a 3D adversarial object into a driving scene to erase targets in BEV) exists in [17]; the contributions here are mesh-vs-NeRF representation, an occlusion module, and the BEV feature loss, each of which is a reasonable but not fundamental advance.

strengths: Novel and clearly motivated threat model: the paper defines a non-invasive, 3D-consistent, universal adversarial object ('rogue mesh') attack for BEV 3D detectors, which is a genuinely under-explored setting compared to invasive camouflage/patch attacks (Fig. 1, Sec. 2), and it articulates why the invasive paradigm is impractical (requires physical access, not scalable).

Technically sensible pipeline with distinct components: automatic mesh placement from 3D bounding boxes (Sec. 3.2), differentiable rendering with PyTorch3D for multi-view consistency, a two-stage (2D overlap + BEV convex-hull) occlusion-aware module with SAM2-derived masks (Sec. 3.3, supplementary Fig. 7), and a BEV feature-based scene confusion loss (Sec. 3.4).

Extensive and fairly thorough empirical evaluation: three victim detectors (BEVDet, BEVDet4D, BEVFormer) on full nuScenes, comparisons with Adv3D (Tab. 2) and UAP (Tab. 3) with explicit discussion of unfair-setting caveats, ablations over shape initialization, training distance, loss components (Tab. 7), and color vs. geometry optimization (Tab. 8).

Beyond-the-core analyses strengthen the case: black-box transfer attacks (Tabs. 9-10), attacks on a LiDAR-supervised camera-only model (GeoBEV, Tab. 14), a robust/adversarially-trained model (Tab. 15), distance robustness (Tabs. 12-13), and scaling with number of randomly placed meshes (Tab. 6).

Physical-world proof of concept (Sec. 4.5, Sec. 11) with a print-aware two-stage optimization and TV regularization, demonstrating localization errors, false positives, cross-view corruption, and misclassification on real captures; the authors honestly discuss the physical-to-digital gap (print gamut issues).

The scientific finding that BEV models are over-reliant on contextual co-occurrence priors (e.g., pedestrian-like textures emerging on adversarial meshes) is an interesting and useful insight for robustness evaluation.
weaknesses: Threat model practicality is overstated in places: mesh placement requires ground-truth 3D annotations of target vehicles, and optimization is white-box (full access to detector internals and BEV features). The universal/transfer results mitigate this somewhat, but the attacker's knowledge assumptions deserve more explicit discussion and justification.

The attribution of the Init-to-Adv performance drop to 'manipulation of contextual reasoning about object co-occurrence' is an interpretation rather than a demonstrated mechanism; no targeted analysis (e.g., probing, feature visualization quantification, or controlled semantic ablations) directly validates the contextual-prior claim.
The scene confusion loss contributes only marginally in the ablation (Adv mAP 0.1311 -> 0.1298 in Tab. 7), which weakens one of the three claimed technical contributions.

Notational/technical sloppiness: Eq. (8) defines Lsim as the cosine similarity but Eq. (9) minimizes it (which would maximize similarity), suggesting a missing sign; Eq. (6)-(7) use informal notation (e.g., 'f(Iadv)confidence x R', 'f(Iadv)B'); minor errors such as 'Sec. 13 also analyze' and inconsistent citation labels (GeoBEV cited as [11]).

Baselines are not directly comparable in threat setting (as the authors admit): Adv3D is a NeRF vehicle-generation attack and UAP is an invasive patch; the comparison tables conflate differences in initialization/object placement with attack efficacy, so the headline 'Drop' percentages (41.4%/55.6%) partially reflect a cleaner experimental protocol rather than a like-for-like algorithmic advantage.

The occlusion module relies on SAM2 masks prompted by GT 2D boxes and a BEV convex-hull heuristic; this is an approximation of true occlusion and its realism/computational cost in dynamic multi-object scenes is not fully characterized.

The physical experiment is a proof of concept with a single camera moved sequentially (not a synchronized six-camera rig), and only qualitative results are shown for the physical attack, so real-world quantitative effectiveness remains uncertain.

Reproducibility details are partially available (supplementary gives hyperparameters, GPU setup, training times), but no code/project-page link is provided in the manuscript ('Project page:' is blank), which limits verifiability for a paper making strong security claims.

strengths: The proposed threat model — a non-invasive, 3D-consistent adversarial object placed in the scene rather than attached to the target vehicle — is a meaningful and largely underexplored direction for evaluating BEV 3D detectors, and the paper's framing of 'scene-level inter-object attacks' is clearly articulated.

The technical pipeline is reasonably complete: differentiable mesh rendering for multi-view consistency (PyTorch3D), a two-stage (2D overlap + BEV convex-hull) occlusion determination procedure, SAM2-based mask compositing, and a BEV feature-space scene-confusion loss. The BEV occlusion/visibility-cone formulation (Eq. 3) is a sensible solution to depth ambiguity.

The evaluation is broad: three victim models (BEVDet, BEVDet4D, BEVFormer), ablations over shape, distance, loss components, color vs. geometry, random-placement scaling, LiDAR-supervised camera-only models (GeoBEV), transfer attacks, a defense-enhanced model, and an extended supplementary with additional metrics and visualizations.

The paper is commendably transparent about confounds: it explicitly separates the 'Clean → Init' (benign occlusion) drop from the 'Init → Adv' (adversarial) drop in Table 1, which is the right way to present such results.

A proof-of-concept physical experiment is included, along with an honest discussion of the physical-to-digital gap (print gamut issues) and print-aware training adaptations (TV loss, lighting simulation).
weaknesses: The threat model's practicality — the paper's central selling point — is undermined by heavy reliance on ground-truth information. Mesh placement requires 3D bounding-box annotations of target vehicles (Sec. 3.2), and the occlusion module requires annotated scene objects {O_k} and their masks at both training and inference time. A real attacker would not have calibrated 3D annotations; this makes the claimed 'far more practical and insidious' threat model considerably less plausible than argued.

The benign-occlusion confound is large. Inserting a plain gray cylinder already drops BEVDet NDS from 0.3942 to 0.3579 (mAP 0.3086 to 0.2625). The marginal adversarial effect (Init → Adv) is real but substantially smaller than the headline drops (e.g., 41.4% NDS drop) suggest, since a significant portion of the degradation is simply from adding any occluding object at 0.1 m from the vehicle — a placement that is arguably quasi-invasive in practice (essentially touching the target).

Transferability results in the supplementary (Tabs. 9–10) are weak, e.g., a BEVDet-optimized mesh reduces BEVFormer NDS only from 0.4592 to 0.4049. Since the attack is fundamentally white-box and transfers poorly, its practical security relevance is limited, yet the paper's conclusions about systemic vulnerability are stated broadly.

Comparisons with baselines are not apples-to-apples. The Adv3D comparison (Tab. 2) is conducted under the authors' own re-implemented setting rather than Adv3D's protocol, and the UAP comparison (Tab. 3) is explicitly acknowledged to be conceptually different; interpreting higher ASR at low IoU thresholds as evidence of superiority involves argument rather than controlled evidence.

The physical experiment is qualitative only. It uses a single tripod-mounted camera sequentially moved through hexagonal positions (not a synchronized surround-view rig), reports no quantitative physical metrics (e.g., physical-world ASR), and validates on a very small number of scenes. Claims of 'physical-world effectiveness' are therefore only weakly supported.

Scene-level attacks require many meshes (4 during training due to memory limits, 15 at test time; Tab. 6 needs up to 10 randomly placed meshes to reach high ASR). This weakens the scalability argument used to criticize invasive attacks, and the paper's own admission that 'deployment cost and complexity' increase is at odds with the framing.

The 'first framework' claim is overstated: non-invasive environmental attacks for BEV detectors already exist (e.g., ground-poster attacks [39], hallucinated-object patches [38]), and the novelty is incremental over Adv3D [15] — mainly replacing NeRF-based texture optimization with mesh rendering plus an occlusion module and a feature-level loss.

Reproducibility is a concern: no code release or project page content is indicated (the project page link is empty), training requires 8×L40 GPUs for up to 57 hours per model, and several details (exact ASR detection protocol, IoU matching, hyperparameter sensitivity beyond α=β=10) are under-specified. There are also writing/presentation defects (e.g., 'Sec. 13 also analyze', inconsistent section numbering between main text and supplementary).

strengths: The paper introduces a well-motivated and practically relevant threat model: non-invasive, scene-level, 3D-consistent adversarial objects for BEV detectors. The Clean/Init/Adv experimental decomposition (Tab. 1) is a thoughtful design that separates benign occlusion effects from the actual adversarial effect, addressing a common confound in physical attack evaluation.

The technical pipeline is reasonably well-engineered: differentiable rendering (PyTorch3D) for multi-view consistency, a two-stage occlusion check (2D box overlap + BEV convex-hull visibility cone) that correctly resolves depth ambiguity (Sec. 8), SAM2-based mask updates, and a painter's-algorithm composition for multiple meshes. The BEV feature-level scene confusion loss is a sensible addition beyond bounding-box-level objectives.

The experimental coverage is broad and above average for attack papers: three victim detectors (BEVDet, BEVDet4D, BEVFormer), white-box and black-box transfer results (Tab. 9-10), shape/distance/placement ablations (Tab. 4-6, 12-13), attacks on LiDAR-supervised camera-only models (GeoBEV, Tab. 14), an adversarial-training defense evaluation (Tab. 15), and a physical-world proof-of-concept with print-aware optimization (TV loss, lighting perturbation stages).

The analysis of emergent semantics (pedestrian-like textures on objects optimized for BEVFormer, cone-like features on cubes) offers an interesting interpretability angle, and the observation that a non-adversarial cylinder alone already degrades performance is an honest disclosure that strengthens credibility.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons are not apples-to-apples, and the paper essentially concedes this. The Adv3D comparison (Tab. 2) benefits from a different (arguably flawed) evaluation setting, and the UAP comparison (Tab. 3) is explicitly run under a modified 'Ours without Real Occ' configuration. While the authors argue these choices are equitable, the quantitative superiority claims over prior work rest on non-standard, author-defined comparison protocols rather than a shared benchmark.

The threat model relies on privileged information that weakens real-world plausibility: mesh placement uses ground-truth 3D bounding box annotations, and occluder identification uses GT 3D annotations of scene objects. The paper does not adequately discuss how the attack would work without oracle access to the scene's annotated geometry.

The physical validation is proof-of-concept only: a single ZED2i camera sequentially placed at six hexagon vertices emulates the six-camera rig (not synchronized, not on a vehicle), and the physical results are qualitative (Fig. 6, 9) with a reported digital-to-physical performance gap. Quantitative physical-world ASR/mAP numbers are absent.

Presentation has notable flaws: broken or vague cross-references ('See Sec. 7', 'schematic in Sec. 8', 'Sec. 13 also analyze the LiDAR-supervised...' with grammatical errors), an empty 'Project page' link, informally specified losses (Eq. 6-7 lack precise definitions of the confidence-space projection R and how predicted boxes in region B are extracted), and Eq. 2 returning an intersection of boxes rather than a scalar as used in the text.

The novelty claim of 'first' 3D-consistent non-invasive attack is somewhat overstated relative to Adv3D [15] and the ground-poster attack of [39]; the contribution is a meaningful refinement (true mesh insertion with occlusion handling and BEV feature losses) rather than an entirely new problem formulation.

Attack strength under the most realistic configuration (with Real Occ) drops considerably (e.g., BEVFormer ASR0.3 falls from 0.405 to 0.245), and single-mesh random placement is weak (ASR0.3 = 0.175 in Tab. 6), indicating the attack's practical effectiveness may require favorable deployment conditions (many visible meshes at close range).
